articles.author: Aabhas Sao
articles.description:
Something clicked for me recently when I was staring at this line in my codebase:
import Button from "../../../../../../components/Button.tsx"

Six levels deep. And honestly, what does that even tell you? You have to mentally trace backwards from wherever you currently are just to figure out where that file lives. The path is relative to this file, which means it looks different in every single file that imports the same component.
There is a cleaner way.
import Button from "@/components/Button.tsx"

Same component. But now the path is absolute, it reads clearly, and it looks identical no matter which file you paste it into. You immediately know where to find it in the project. No counting ../ hops.
It takes about five minutes. In your tsconfig.json:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "baseUrl":…
articles.title: Stop Writing ../../../../../../ in Your Imports

articles.description:
I recently built a small tool called Forge STA (Speech-To-Action).
The idea is simple:

Speech should not just become text.

Speech should become actions.

So instead of:

Speech → Text

we get:  
Speech → Text → CLI → Anything  
Most speech tools stop at transcription.

You dictate something and it becomes text.

But developers often want something different:  
turn speech into code comments

generate prompts

trigger scripts

pipe into tools

format into HTML / Markdown / XML



In short:  
Speech should be part of a toolchain.  
Forge STA uses a very simple design.
Mic
 ↓
Speech Recognition
 ↓
Post Processing (CLI)
 ↓
Output / Action

The interesting part is that post-processing is external.

No plugins.

No internal scripting.

Just CLI tools.

Example:
STA → python formatter.py
STA → …

This blog post was created for the Gemini Live Agent Challenge hackathon.

Imagine trying to find an apartment on Zillow without seeing the screen. A sighted user glances at a map, scans listings, clicks filters — all in seconds. A visually impaired user faces a different reality: tab through dozens of invisible elements, hope the screen reader can parse Zillow's React-rendered layout, and guess which button says "Apply Filters" versus "Clear All." Over 2.2 billion people worldwide live with visual impairment, and for many of them, this is what browsing the web feels like every day.
Despite decades of work on web accessibility standards, screen readers still fundamentally struggle with the modern web…

articles.author: Anubhav Rai
articles.description:
Most uptime monitors tell you your API is down. Mine tells you why.
Most monitors do something like this:
const response = await axios.get(url);


That tells you nothing. You know the request failed. You don't know where.
Switching to native http with timing hooks
const req = transport.request(options, (res) => {


req.on('socket', (socket) => {


Now every ping stores dns_lookup_ms, tcp_connect_ms, tls_handshake_ms, and ttfb_ms separately in the database alongside the usual status_code and response_time_ms
The inference logic
// DNS spiked but TCP was fine — DNS issue


// TCP failed entirely — server unreachable


// Everything fine until TTFB — server-side problem


// Status code tells us exactly what happened


No ML, no black box. Just rule-based inference against a baseline. A 503 with normal DNS/TCP/TLS timings but a spiked TTFB looks completely different from a connection timeout with no TCP at all.
What it looks like in practice
When a monitor goes down, instead of just logging the failure, Pulse shows:
Root Cause Analysis
DNS Lookup      → 34ms   normal

TLS Handshake   → 71ms   normal
Suggestion: Server is responding but very slowly —
The baseline problem
What I learned
Pulse is free — 5 monitors, no credit card. If you want to see the root cause analysis in action or poke around the implementation: Pulse
Happy to hear opinions!
